<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line" lang="en">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Anthony Bao
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Electrical &amp; Computer Engineering, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712, USA

</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jeffrey Lai
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>The Oden Institute, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712, USA

</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">William Gilpin
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:wgilpin@utexas.edu">wgilpin@utexas.edu</a>
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Physics, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712, USA

</span></span></span></span></div>
<div class="ltx_dates">August 24, 2026</div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Large-scale foundation models for scientific machine learning adapt to physical settings unseen during training, such as zero-shot transfer between turbulent scales.
This phenomenon, in-context learning, challenges conventional understanding of learning and adaptation in physical systems.
Here, we study in-context learning of dynamical systems in a minimal setting: we train a small two-layer, single-head transformer to forecast one dynamical system, and then evaluate its ability to forecast a <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">different</span> dynamical system without retraining.
We discover an early tradeoff in training between in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance, which manifests as a secondary double descent phenomenon.
We discover that attention models apply a transfer-operator forecasting strategy in-context. They (1) lift low-dimensional time series using delay embedding, to detect the system’s higher-dimensional dynamical manifold, and (2) identify and forecast long-lived invariant sets that characterize the global flow on this manifold.
Our results clarify the mechanism enabling large pretrained models to forecast unseen physical systems at test without retraining, and they illustrate the unique ability of attention-based models to leverage global attractor information in service of short-term forecasts.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p">Scientific foundation models are pretrained on vast amounts of data, with a goal of discovering generalizable patterns applicable to unseen problem domains.
Animating such efforts is the observation that, at sufficient scale, these models exhibit the emergent capability to solve unseen tasks during testing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>. For example, models trained on low-resolution turbulent snapshots exhibit the spontaneous ability to forecast higher-resolution grids <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>. In some cases, models trained on certain classes of PDEs, like diffusion equations, develop the ability to forecast new classes of PDEs, like wave equations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>. These findings align with similar observations for large language models, which exhibit the emergent ability to solve unseen tasks, like novel logical puzzles or mathematical derivations, at sufficient scale <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p2.1" class="ltx_p">The underlying mechanism, in-context learning, differs from classical machine learning approaches that dichotomize learning during training from testing during inference.
Instead, pretraining provides a sufficiently large model with vast background experience and an underlying world model, allowing it to quickly adapt to new tasks based on minimal context <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>.
In traditional scientific machine learning, a trained model acts as a surrogate for the dynamical process that generated the training data, and so a trained model can, at best, only generate test outputs matching the distribution of the training data, known as <span id="p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">in-distribution (ID) generalization</span>.
In contrast, in-context learning enables <span id="p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization</span> on new data distributions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>.
However, the underlying mechanisms enabling in-context learning and OOD generalization in SciML are poorly understood, even as recent empirical studies have uncovered robust signatures of generalization in areas as diverse as turbulence closure modelling, large eddy convection, or magnetohydrodynamics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p3.1" class="ltx_p">To clarify the origin of in-context learning in scientific machine learning, we draw inspiration from recent works that train minimal language models, in order to probe the mechanistic origin of in-context learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>. We train a small transformer model on a univariate trajectory originating from a single dynamical system (denoted Train-ID), and we then evaluate its ability to both (1) forecast a different trajectory from the <span id="p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">same</span> dynamical system (Test-ID), and (2) forecast a trajectory from a <span id="p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">different</span> dynamical system (Test-OOD). We first generate a trajectory <math id="p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>D</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{D}</annotation></semantics></math> from the <math id="p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional ordinary differential equation <math id="p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dot{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>˙</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dot{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y})</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}(0)=\mathbf{y}_{0}^{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐲</mi><mn>0</mn><mtext>train</mtext></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}(0)=\mathbf{y}_{0}^{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Train-ID consists of a univariate training time series <math id="p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> representing evenly-spaced samples of the first coordinate of the full trajectory <math id="p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}(t)</annotation></semantics></math>. In order to use language modeling approaches, we convert these continuous values to discrete tokens by uniformly quantizing them into <math id="p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> evenly-spaced bins (token IDs). This same approach is used by leading foundation models for zero-shot time series forecasting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. For simplicity, hereafter we use <math id="p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> to refer to elements of the tokenized univariate time series.</p>
</div>
<div id="p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p4.1" class="ltx_p">A probabilistic forecast model <math id="p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}(x_{t+1}|\mathbf{x}_{C})\in\mathbb{R}^{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>V</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}(x_{t+1}|\mathbf{x}_{C})\in\mathbb{R}^{V}</annotation></semantics></math> accepts the context vector <math id="p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{C}\in\mathbb{Z}^{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>C</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{C}\in\mathbb{Z}^{C}</annotation></semantics></math> comprising <math id="p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> past tokens, and returns a vector <math id="p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}(x_{t+1})\in\mathbb{R}^{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>V</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}(x_{t+1})\in\mathbb{R}^{V}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponding to next-token probabilities across the vocabulary. Following prior works on minimal transformers, we model <math id="p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}</annotation></semantics></math> using a minimal GPT-like transformer, comprising two layers with a single attention head each, and relative positional encoding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> (<a href="#S2" title="Appendix B Model architecture and training ‣ Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix B</span></a>).
For each input context <math id="p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{C}</annotation></semantics></math>, transformers compute self-attention, comprising <math id="p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> pairwise comparisons among all tokens in the context, resulting in attention weights <math id="p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A(\mathbf{x}_{C})\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A(\mathbf{x}_{C})\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times C}</annotation></semantics></math> that quantify the relative importance of each past token in influencing the next-token probabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p5.1" class="ltx_p">We train the transformer <math id="p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}(x_{t+1}|\mathbf{x}_{C})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}(x_{t+1}|\mathbf{x}_{C})</annotation></semantics></math> on Train-ID using standard gradient-based optimization with cross-entropy loss, which aligns <math id="p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}(x_{t+1}|\mathbf{x}_{C})\in\mathbb{R}^{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>V</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}(x_{t+1}|\mathbf{x}_{C})\in\mathbb{R}^{V}</annotation></semantics></math> with the empirical next-token distribution <math id="p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x_{t+1}|\mathbf{x}_{C})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x_{t+1}|\mathbf{x}_{C})</annotation></semantics></math> in the training data.
After training, multistep forecasts are generated by sampling tokens from the transformer <math id="p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{x}_{t+1}\sim\hat{p}(x_{t+1}|\mathbf{x}_{C})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{x}_{t+1}\sim\hat{p}(x_{t+1}|\mathbf{x}_{C})</annotation></semantics></math> and appending each sample to the context autoregressively.
Throughout training, we measure the transformer’s ability to forecast an unseen trajectory from the same dynamical system (Test-ID) denoted <math id="p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dot{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>˙</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dot{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y})</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}(0)=\mathbf{y}_{0}^{\text{test}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐲</mi><mn>0</mn><mtext>test</mtext></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}(0)=\mathbf{y}_{0}^{\text{test}}</annotation></semantics></math> as well as its ability to forecast a trajectory from an unseen system (Test-OOD) denoted <math id="p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dot{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{y})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>˙</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dot{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{y})</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}(0)=\mathbf{y}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝐲</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}(0)=\mathbf{y}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>. We repeat all experiments by training new transformers on each of <math id="p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math> different pairs of systems drawn from a large database of ordinary differential equations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>, allowing measurement across a variety of distinct physical systems.</p>
</div>
<div id="p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p6.1" class="ltx_p">Remarkably, we observe that, in this minimal setting, small pretrained transformers exhibit the ability to predict unseen dynamical systems (Fig. <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>A). These forecasts exceed the quality of naive baselines like mean regression, suggesting that transformers employ a more sophisticated in-context forecast strategy by leveraging their uniquely long context.
During training on a single system (Train-ID), we see an early underfitting-to-overfitting transition on Test-ID, consistent with the classical bias-variance tradeoff: the model initially learns generalizable information about the system’s dynamics, leading to improvements on both seen and unseen data (Fig. <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>B, gray and blue curves). However, as the Train-ID loss continues to fall, the model begins to overfit, leading to an increase in Test-ID error. At even later stages of training, we observe epoch-wise double descent, a recently-characterized phenomenon in which the Test-ID error further falls again below the classical bias-variance optimum <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>. However, we discover a <span id="p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">second</span>, earlier double descent curve in the Test-OOD error (Fig. <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>B, magenta curve). This finding implies that information generalizable to other dynamical systems becomes available to the transformer during the pretraining process, but that it is bounded from above by ID-system-specific information.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18679v1/training.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/206;" width="476" height="206" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>
<span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Double descent during in-context learning of dynamical systems.</span>
(A) Forecasts from a transformer trained on univariate time series from one dynamical system (Train-ID) then evaluated on its ability to forecast unseen trajectories from the same system (Test-ID, blue), versus forecasts of trajectories from an unseen system (Test-OOD, magenta). Gray curve shows the context, a subset of the total training data.
(B) Loss curves on the training data, versus held-out in-distribution and out-of-distribution validation sets.
Ranges are standard errors across <math id="S0.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math> replicate experiments, each corresponding to a different randomly-sampled train/test pair of dynamical systems.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p7.1" class="ltx_p">Where does this generalization signal come from?
We sample the transformer’s time-delayed conditional distribution <math id="p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}(x_{t+1}|x_{t-k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}(x_{t+1}|x_{t-k})</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\leq C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\leq C</annotation></semantics></math> averaged across Test-OOD for all lag values <math id="p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\in 0,1,...,C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\in 0,1,...,C</annotation></semantics></math>. We find that this distribution qualitatively resembles the true attractor of Test-OOD, implying that the univariate model identifies relevant information about the unobserved multivariate attractor during testing (Fig. <a href="#S0.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>A).
This result is consistent with Takens’ theorem: a univariate time series arising from an attractor with intrinsic dimension <math id="p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathcal{M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathcal{M}}</annotation></semantics></math> can be embedded using <math id="p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{E}=2d_{\mathcal{M}}+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>E</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{E}=2d_{\mathcal{M}}+1</annotation></semantics></math> time delays. We thus refer to the time delay coordinates <math id="p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{i}=[\mathbf{x}_{i-d_{E}},...,\mathbf{x}_{i}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>E</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{i}=[\mathbf{x}_{i-d_{E}},...,\mathbf{x}_{i}]</annotation></semantics></math> as an estimate of the unobserved true phase space coordinates <math id="p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐲</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p8.1" class="ltx_p">To test the scaling predicted by Takens’ theorem, we generate new Test-OOD trajectories using the Lorenz-96 system, a dynamical system with a controllable number of dynamical variables <math id="p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>. This system’s manifold dimension <math id="p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathcal{M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathcal{M}}</annotation></semantics></math> scales approximately linearly with <math id="p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> (<a href="#S4" title="Appendix D Estimating the manifold dimension of the Lorenz-96 system ‣ Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix D</span></a>).
As we vary the number of dynamical variables in Test-OOD <math id="p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=3,4,...25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=3,4,...25</annotation></semantics></math>, we evaluate the average Test-OOD accuracy of transformers originally trained on a different dynamical system (Train-ID) with <math id="p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=3</annotation></semantics></math>.
For each test case, we compare the transformer’s empirical order-<math id="p8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> conditional distribution (averaged across Test-OOD) to a <math id="p8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-order Markov chain <math id="p8.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x_{t+1}|x_{t},x_{t-1},...,x_{t-k-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x_{t+1}|x_{t},x_{t-1},...,x_{t-k-1})</annotation></semantics></math> trained directly on Test-OOD, in order to estimate the effective order <math id="p8.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> of the Markov chain best-approximating the transformer’s Test-OOD dynamics.
We find that the order of the best-approximating Markov chain scales with the intrinsic dimension of Test-OOD (Fig. <a href="#S0.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>C). This finding is striking, because the univariate Test-OOD series contains no direct information about the true dimensionality <math id="p8.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="p8.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathcal{M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathcal{M}}</annotation></semantics></math>, suggesting that the transformer instead leverages information from time delay embedding in-context.</p>
</div>
<div id="p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p9.1" class="ltx_p">To confirm that this effect arises from the transformer’s internal representations, for each Test-OOD example, we calculate the attention rollout matrix <math id="p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{\text{roll}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mtext>roll</mtext></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{\text{roll}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times C}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>. This metric measures the sparsity of the model’s attention to different token positions, averaged across the entire testing set and both attention heads.
We compute the stable rank of the rollout matrix (<math id="p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{latent}}=\text{srank}(A_{\text{roll}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>latent</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>srank</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mtext>roll</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{latent}}=\text{srank}(A_{\text{roll}})</annotation></semantics></math>) as a measure of the intrinsic dimensionality of the transformer’s latent representations.
We find that increasing attractor dimension <math id="p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathcal{M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathcal{M}}</annotation></semantics></math> strongly correlates with increasing latent dimensionality <math id="p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{latent}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>latent</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{latent}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Because the univariate time series presented to the transformer lack direct information about dimensionality, we conclude that the trained model infers information about the underlying attractor via in-context learning.
Thus, not only does the transformer embed the test time series, it does so adaptively by identifying when a univariate time series arises from a high-dimensional system.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S0.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18679v1/embedding.png" id="S0.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/473;" width="476" height="473" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>
<span id="S0.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Transformers perform time-delay embedding during inference.</span>
(A) Empirical time-delayed next-token probabilities <math id="S0.F2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{model}}(x_{t+1}|x_{t-k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>model</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{model}}(x_{t+1}|x_{t-k})</annotation></semantics></math> averaged across Test-OOD context for a transformer trained on a different system (Train-ID).
(B) Exact next-token probabilities <math id="S0.F2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{true}}(x_{t+1}|x_{t-k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>true</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{true}}(x_{t+1}|x_{t-k})</annotation></semantics></math> obtained from fitting a Markov chain on a long sample of Test-OOD.
(C) The order of the closest-approximating Markov chain, versus the true intrinsic dimension <math id="S0.F2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathcal{M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathcal{M}}</annotation></semantics></math> of the full attractor from which the univariate Test-OOD trajectory originates.
(D) The effective dimension (stable rank) of the transformer’s attention rollout matrix versus the true intrinsic dimension of Test-OOD.
Each point is an average over <math id="S0.F2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math> replicate models trained on a different low-dimensional dynamical system.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p10.1" class="ltx_p">We next consider how the model pushes forward the dynamics on the dynamical coordinates <math id="p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{y}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Broadly, there are two ways that a surrogate model could represent a dynamical propagator, given finite-length context: (1) a differential form based on approximating time derivatives (as in multi-step integrators, or differential equation inference methods like SINDy), or (2) an integral approach that approximates a transfer operator (as in neural operators or discrete-time system identification) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.
Based on the coincidence of the trained model’s empirical logit distribution with a Markov chain, we hypothesize the latter: transformers approximate propagators in-context.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S0.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18679v1/operator.png" id="S0.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/414;" width="476" height="414" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>
<span id="S0.F3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Transformers learn in-context transfer operators on reconstructed dynamical manifolds.</span>
(A) (Top) The true invariant distribution (<math id="S0.F3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{(0)}(\mathbf{y})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{(0)}(\mathbf{y})</annotation></semantics></math>) and longest-lived metastable distributions (<math id="S0.F3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{(i)}(\mathbf{y})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{(i)}(\mathbf{y})</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="S0.F3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, almost-invariant sets) estimated from the fully-observed state space as the leading eigenvectors of the fully-observed transfer operator <math id="S0.F3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\mathbf{y}_{t+1}|\mathbf{y}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐲</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐲</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\mathbf{y}_{t+1}|\mathbf{y}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> (ranked by <math id="S0.F3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left|\lambda_{i}\right|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left|\lambda_{i}\right|</annotation></semantics></math>).
(Bottom) The invariant and metastable distributions of the transformer, based on its next-token prediction probabilities over time-delayed univariate Test-OOD input sequences. Distributions are estimated as the leading eigenvectors of the lag-<math id="S0.F3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> conditional probabilities <math id="S0.F3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}(x_{t+1}...x_{t-K+2}|x_{t}...x_{t-K+1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}(x_{t+1}...x_{t-K+2}|x_{t}...x_{t-K+1})</annotation></semantics></math> derived from the transformer probabilities. Because the transformer is univariate, eigenvectors are plotted on the time-delay embedding <math id="S0.F3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{y}}\equiv[x_{t},...,x_{t-K}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>≡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{y}}\equiv[x_{t},...,x_{t-K}]</annotation></semantics></math>.
(B) The eigenvalue spectrum of the transfer operator estimated from the fully-observed attractor, and the implicit transfer operator of the transformer.
(C) The KL divergence between the ground-truth invariant distribution of the transfer operator, and transformer empirical operator’s distribution, versus both Test-OOD validation loss and training epoch (color). A 95% confidence interval linear fit is underlaid (blue).
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p11.1" class="ltx_p">To test this hypothesis, we extract the empirical transition matrix of the transformer on the space of length-<math id="p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> delay vectors <math id="p11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> by aggregating multi-step predictions from the model <math id="p11.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}(x_{t+1}\mid\mathbf{x}_{C})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}(x_{t+1}\mid\mathbf{x}_{C})</annotation></semantics></math>. Briefly, across Test-OOD we tabulate each distinct <math id="p11.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-gram (<math id="p11.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="p11.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k&lt;C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k&lt;C</annotation></semantics></math>), and we group together all context sequences <math id="p11.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{C}</annotation></semantics></math> that end in that <math id="p11.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-gram. For each unique <math id="p11.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-gram, we randomly-sample from all matching context sequences and predict the frequency of the next token <math id="p11.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math>. By repeating this process separately for each <math id="p11.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-gram, we can estimate a transfer operator on the time-delayed sequence <math id="p11.m12" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p(\mathbf{\hat{y}}_{t+1}\mid\mathbf{\hat{y}}_{t})\equiv p(x_{t+1},x_{t},...,x_{t-k}|x_{t},x_{t-1},...,x_{t-k-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≡</mo><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\mathbf{\hat{y}}_{t+1}\mid\mathbf{\hat{y}}_{t})\equiv p(x_{t+1},x_{t},...,x_{t-k}|x_{t},x_{t-1},...,x_{t-k-1})</annotation></semantics></math>.
This row-stochastic transition matrix describes the model-implied dynamics on the lag-<math id="p11.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> state space embedding of the univariate Test-OOD time series.</p>
</div>
<div id="p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p12.1" class="ltx_p">We compare the empirical operator to the ground truth operator <math id="p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\mathbf{y}_{t+1}\mid\mathbf{y}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐲</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>𝐲</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\mathbf{y}_{t+1}\mid\mathbf{y}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, which we estimate from the <span id="p12.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">fully-observed</span> state space using Ulam’s method, which discretizes the full multivariate phase space and tabulates all transition rates between pairs of regions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>.
We observe that the leading eigenvalues (ranked by <math id="p12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left|\lambda_{i}\right|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left|\lambda_{i}\right|</annotation></semantics></math>) closely match, implying that the transformer captures the dominant timescales associated with the Perron-Frobenius operator propagating the dynamics (Fig. <a href="#S0.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>B).
The corresponding eigenfunctions represent the stationary distribution <math id="p12.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{(0)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{(0)}</annotation></semantics></math> and subleading eigenfunctions <math id="p12.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{(1)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{(1)}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="p12.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{(2)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{(2)}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponding to long-lived metastable trapping regions, known as <span id="p12.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">almost-invariant sets</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>. These eigenfunctions occur in pairs due to symmetry (Fig. <a href="#S0.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>A).</p>
</div>
<div id="p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p13.1" class="ltx_p">To confirm that the onset of OOD generalization during training arises from test-time inference of the underlying propagator, we directly compare the Test-OOD loss to the KL divergence <math id="p13.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="D_{KL}(\pi^{(0)}\parallel\hat{\pi}^{(0)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>π</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{KL}(\pi^{(0)}\parallel\hat{\pi}^{(0)})</annotation></semantics></math> between the true and model-implied invariant distributions.
Across hundreds of unique pairs of systems, we observe consistent correlation between Test-OOD loss and distributional distance (Fig. <a href="#S0.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>C).
We thus conclude that, as the transformer’s out-of-distribution performance improves, it learns in-context an increasingly accurate estimate of the Perron-Frobenius operator of the fully-observed true system.</p>
</div>
<div id="p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p14.1" class="ltx_p">Taken together, our results show that, during inference, transformers trained on dynamical systems first learn to perform time delay embedding on the context, and then use co-occurrence statistics to approximate the true transfer operator of the fully-observed state space.
Our work thus provides an example of how a learning model can extract a system-independent forecasting strategy despite system-specific training, beyond naive strategies observed in prior works such as parroting sequences from the context <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>.
Our work thus provides a potential explanation for recent works showing the surprising ability of pretrained foundation models to forecast dynamical systems outside their training data, such as turbulent flows, weather fronts, or plasma dynamics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>.
Additionally, our observation of in-context time delay embedding supports findings throughout the broader time series literature, that univariate models often match the performance of multivariate models, even for datasets with strong covariates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>.
It also accords with a recent theoretical result showing that single-layer transformers can implement adaptive time-delay embedding in-context, given sufficient latent dimensionality <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>.
Finally, our results support recent neural scaling laws showing improved performance of time series and scientific foundation models with additional context <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>.
Reminiscent of similar findings in language models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, our work demonstrates how the unique quadratic complexity of attention-based models enables the emergence of nontrivial strategies for estimating and propagating dynamical states.</p>
</div>

<span class="ltx_bibblock ltx_bib_cited">Cited by: <a href="#p14.1" title="Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context</span></a>.
</span></li>
